A SATURDAY CAUSERIE.

In things that matter — by which are now generally accepted questions relating to the strike and the boycott—Hongkong has had another quiet week. "Nothing new" is the order of each day, although there is gradually arising a quiet under-current of greater confidence than has been known for some months. One important piece of intelligence is that the Finance Committee of the Legislative Council is to consider on Monday the advisability of re-opening the Statistical Department of the Imports and Exports Office, the closing of which some time ago was decided upon by the Government in connection with its economy campaign. Strong representations have been made by the General Chamber of Commerce in favour of re-opening the Department. There are other factors than the mere momentary saving of a few thousand dollars to be taken into consideration. It is known that the Colony has suffered trade losses through the strike and the boycott; but naturally it is impossible to assess these properly without a Statistical Department, nor can comparisons be made in the current year with previous periods unless that Department is functioning. In short, it would appear to be nothing short of false economy to delay the re-opening. In other purely local affairs, the annual Race meeting has, as usual, been responsible for good displays of sportsmanship, not to mention the attraction to thousands of the inevitable cash sweeps. And mention may also be made of the latest success of the Hongkong A.D.C. in its staging of "If."
In the domain of Imperial questions a good start has been made with the flight from Cairo to the Cape undertaken by the Royal Air Force, but it was, unfortunate that the aeroplane flight from Karachi to London had to be abandoned on the Persian coast owing to acute fatigue trouble after a struggle against sand storms and mist. On the international horizon only one question has loomed largely—the controversy over the Council of the League of Nations and its enlargement either with the admission of Germany or over and above that nation's election to a permanent seat. The Home Press has been "nervy" and hysterical all along, nothing being said by Sir Austen Chamberlain in his long speech in the House of Commons on Thursday to soothe the ruffled feelings of his Press and political critics. As stated in effect in this column yesterday, in commenting on China's application for a permanent seat on the League Council, nothing is to be gained by "crossing the bridge before we come to it" for it will indeed come as a distinct surprise if the claims of nations other than Germany are disposed of at this month's meeting at Geneva. But, by being deferred till September, those other claims will stand immeasurably to gain by being considered in an atmosphere more akin to cordiality and goodwill than that of the moment. In regard to other foreign affairs, China's civil wars are once again providing the Northern papers with plenty of material. The stage has been set for another clash of arms between the rival war lords, among whom the "Christian" General, Feng Yu-shiang, has once again emerged from his brief period of obscurity and taken the field with the Kuominchun forces. We may soon expect to see the establishment of a Naval Volunteer Defence Corps, a fact accomplished. We should like to say the same of a Police Reserve. The absence of this Reserve has been a minor wonder. During the war the then Reserve did a magnificent work. It accomplished more than it set out to do. It proved how the interesting units of our cosmopolitan life could combine for the common good and meet on the common ground of service. The Reserve was in commonly well directed. It was not merely served by patriotism. Efficiency was aimed at and achieved. It gave interest to those who patrolled, and by its lectures on police law, the problems it put at various examination on procedures in certain circumstances, added to knowledge. It ceased on the conclusion of war to be somewhat half-married. It is directed during the two upheavals which have affected the Colony. LORD WILLINGDON.

CORDIAL WELCOME FROM
ALL CHINESE

The "N.C. Daily News" of last Monday reports — Lord Willingdon, Chairman of the delegation to advise the Statutory Committee with regard to the disposition of the British Boxer Indemnity funds, left yesterday morning about 11 o'clock by the "Haishing". Lord Willingdon was accompanied by Sir Francis Aglen, Inspector General of Customs, and by Mr. R. F. Johnston, secretary of the delegation. It is expected that they will return about the middle of March to meet the other members of the delegation, Dame Adelaide Anderson and Professor Soothill, who are arriving by different routes. Whether the delegation will make Shanghai or Peking the main base for its deliberations is undecided, but it is probable that it will at least open its sittings here.

When seen by a representative of the "North China Daily News," yesterday Lord Willingdon expressed great satisfaction with the results of his visit in Shanghai. "While three days is a short time on which to base an opinion, and while my activities here have been entirely social and not official," said he, "I cannot help feeling that the spirit of kindness and cooperation everywhere manifested is a very happy augury. I have been privileged to meet a great many prominent Chinese gentlemen and personally I have not been able to discover any of that anti-British feeling which has been so widely advertised.

The Chairman of the Chamber of Commerce very graciously gave to luncheon for me, the Chinese Commissioner of Foreign Affairs gave us a dinner party, I had tea with Mr. Tong Shao-yi, and also with Lord Li Ching-mei. At the Consulate-General Mr. Barton has given luncheons and dinner parties at which I have had an opportunity to meet many of the Chinese and I have had interviews with four or five of their prominent leaders. The feeling I have in all these instances is that I have formed contacts with people who are anxious to assist the delegation in making its inquiries and who will be willing to place all their sources of information at its service. Besides all this," he added, "I attended the races and saw for the first time that famous institution, the China-pony, Really, this has been a remarkably pleasant three days."

Sir,—Many times the attempts of authors to represent a Chinese's pronunciation of words with "r" in them have been a cause of slight amusement, but on reading Conrad's "Victory" recently I was amazed to find that he makes a Chinese say "levolve" for "revolver."
The sound of the letter "r" has no difficulty for any Chinese, and is probably the commonest sound in the language, as instanced by the fact that every Chinese is called familiarly by the sound "r" as a prefix to his name, thus Mr. Wong Sing is called R Sing of Ah Sing by his friends. The sound of "r" in the name itself is common, as for example, Chan Harr, a well-known business man in Hongkong, or Mah Lam.

The uneducated classes of Chinese do have a difficulty with the sound "ri" "ra" and "ro" and it is here that the "I" sound would be heard. A coolie speaking of a river would say "liver" but certainly not "livel."
Strangely enough, many Japanese have a difficulty with the "I" sound and would call an aeroplane a "frying machine" instead of "flying machine."

Our former Governor's A Stubb's love of a joke, may Story, possibly be inherited from his father. Here is a story of Bishop Stubbs told by Mr. Pett Ridge. The Bishop reached a village church one Sunday evening. The verger pointed out that his lordship had had a long cross-country journey, that his lordship was about to deliver a sermon, would his lordship permit him to mix for his lordship a good stiff glass of whisky and water.
"No!" said the Bishop firmly. "For three reasons, no. First, that I am, as you say, about to go into the pulpit to preach; second, that I am chairman this year of a temperance society; and, third, that I have just had one!"

The unknown highwayman who rode his horse along Lansdowne-passage and up the stone steps has won immortal fame for his deed. The visitor to the London Museum in remote ages will see the iron bar set up to prevent other gentlemen of the road from doing likewise, and wonder, like Mr. Pickwick, that such things could be. But, in fact, the Lansdowne-passage bargives a miserably inadequate notion of the perils of eighteenth century London. The Lord Mayor presented a petition to George II. against the "evil-disposed persons," armed with dangerous weapons, who "infested notionally the private lanes and passages, but likewise the public streets and places of usual concourse, committing most daring outrages upon his Majesty's subpects." That was in 1744. Half a century was to pass before things grew better. Highwaymen commonly rode into Hyde Park at dusk, fastened their horses to the railings, and went out to stop "chairs, carriages, and pedestrians." In 1749 Horace Walpole coming back by moonlight from Holland House to Arlington-street was stopped in Hyde Park by two gentlemen of the road, and "the pistol of one of them going off accidentally" was within an ace of killing him, and actually grazed his eye. One of these heroes was the great Maclean, "the gentleman highwayman," who went to Tyburn next year. On a Sunday night in that year another attacked a post-chaise in Piccadilly, rode over the watchman, almost killed him, and escaped. Mr. Henry W. Nevison, the veteran journalist, has made the most interesting comment on Father Ronald Knox's broadcasting exploit. When the centenary of Dickens's birth was celebrated in 1912, the late H. W. Massingham, editor of the "Nation," asked Mr. Nevinson to write something about the great novelist Mr. Nevinson proceeded to write a review of "Pickwick" as though it were a new book that had just appeared. It began with the words, "Mr. Dickens will go far," and proceeded to point out some flaws in the composition. Next week the office of the "Nation" was deluged with letters of protest, demanding to know how the editor of the "Nation" and his staff could possibly be ignorant of the fact that the "Pickwick Papers" was not at all a new book, nor was Dickens a young writer. They were solemnly assured that Dickens had been dead some forty-two years. Irony Mr. Nevinson concludes in his letter to the "Manchester Guardian," is a dangerous weapon.

When it grew towards evening a bell was tolled in Kensington Gardens at intervals to give people warning when others were going back to town, that they might form parties strong enough to defend themselves. But your gentleman of the road was not always without his uses. When the younger Pitt was fighting his pitched battle against the Fox and North coalition, he boasted, so the story goes, to a fair Whig dame that one of the Northern county seats was safe: "Five thousand guineas go down to night by a sure hand." "The deuce they do!" said the lady and took counsel with her friends. The Treasury messenger was stopped on the Great North Road by a convenient highwayman. The only incredible thing in the story is that Pitt should have talked freely at a woman.
